distractors.text: hint that the machine is malfunctioning and that the hospice staff have neglected his basic care
distractors.why: Literal reading of a figurative 'complaint'; the text shows weariness, not a malfunction or staff neglect.

distractors.text: reveal that the narrator resents having been summoned to the hospice on a snowy weekday morning
distractors.why: Unsupported: the narrator takes pride in driving in snow; the machine's weariness is not her resentment.

distractors.text: portray the machine as a cheerful companion whose steady sounds soften the gloom of the sickroom
distractors.why: Wrong tone: a 'small complaint' and being overworked are weary, not cheerful or comforting.

distractors.text: the narrator's pride in his city career over the family's farm life
distractors.why: Unsupported: 'I don't salt' is a refusal, but nothing ties salt to a city versus farm contrast.

distractors.text: the church ladies' kindness toward the family in their mourning
distractors.why: Wrong function: Nick uses and moves the shaker; it is never associated with the ladies.

distractors.text: a contest the brothers enjoy playing together as they once did
distractors.why: Literal for figurative: the chess image conveys stalemate, not real enjoyment of a game.

distractors.text: "I had not come to fight. Nick had stayed"
distractors.why: Reversal: offered as proof of good faith, not of the narrator's fault.

distractors.text: "Nick salted his perogies before he tasted them"
distractors.why: Wrong scope: describes Nick's habit, not the narrator's responsibility.

distractors.text: "Darlene was telling the story about the combine"
distractors.why: Unsupported: concerns a cousin's story and says nothing about Teddy's role.

distractors.text: show that their father preferred Teddy over Nick as a boy
distractors.why: Reversal: the joke was meant to make Nick laugh; Teddy was the one left out.

distractors.text: offer a light comic aside apart from the central conflict
distractors.why: Wrong function: the memory directly explains the tension and the refused shaker.

distractors.text: explain why the brothers stopped marking their birthdays
distractors.why: Unsupported: the birthday cards kept coming; nothing suggests birthdays were abandoned.

content.text: Length targets: Q1 key is 74 characters, so each distractor needs roughly 68-83 characters. Q9 key is 117 characters, so each distractor needs roughly 108-131 characters.

distractors.text: devout belief that every kind of pride is a sin, whatever prompts it
distractors.why: Too broad: the text shows no general doctrine; her guilt is tied to this specific deception.

distractors.text: bitterness that the inspector credits the children and overlooks her
distractors.why: Unsupported: no resentment appears; she hides her role and seeks no credit.

distractors.text: relief that the inspection is nearly done and her secret has been kept
distractors.why: Wrong scope: the inspection is not over, and exposure follows immediately after.

distractors.text: Dask's remark reveals his practical knowledge of cloth and his worry that a good garment might be left to spoil unused.
distractors.why: Literal for figurative: it reads the remark only literally, so it cannot support the claim of permission.

distractors.text: The remark warns her that the Ministry will soon take everything from the school, much as moths ruin a coat left hanging.
distractors.why: Reversal: Dask has just passed the school as satisfactory, so the remark is not a threat.

distractors.text: This shows Dask is a generous man, since officials in novels of this kind are so often secretly sympathetic to the poor.
distractors.why: Unsupported: it rests on outside generalizations about fiction rather than on the text.

content.text: Key length is 180 characters, so each distractor should fall between roughly 166 and 202 characters.

distractors.text: Through the decline of the clock shop, the passage argues that small family trades of the period were doomed by the dealers who bought up their stock at very low prices.
distractors.why: Unsupported: Pell is an incidental figure, and the passage makes no argument about the fate of small trades.

distractors.text: Through the father's secret ledger, the passage shows that the narrator was right all along to believe her father cared more for his clocks than for her own company.
distractors.why: Reversal: the ledger shows the opposite, since each clock in it records a moment from her life.

distractors.text: Through its many images of stopped time, the passage suggests that every human memory is unreliable and that no event in the past can ever be known with any confidence.
distractors.why: Too broad: it turns one disputed memory into a universal claim about all memory that the passage does not make.

content.text: Length targets: Q5 key 69 chars, so 63-77. Q7 key 65, so 60-72. Q11 key 49, so 45-55. Q12 key 68, so 63-76.

distractors.text: has abandoned his clerkship and taken up Venn's trade on the water
distractors.why: Leaving his private book unopened is a moral choice, not a career change; he does not become a fisherman.

distractors.text: has grown more convinced that Harrowby's arithmetic is cold and cruel
distractors.why: The kitchen discovery overturns his earlier judgment of Harrowby rather than deepening it.

distractors.text: has decided the Trust's books are falsified to hide its real dealings
distractors.why: 'Figures' and 'left out' sound like fraud, but the passage points to hidden generosity, not dishonesty.

distractors.text: letting the reader enter Venn's private mind as he turns down the offer
distractors.why: Venn's inner thoughts are never shown; only his words and gestures are given.

distractors.text: laying out the inner motives of every character with equal fullness
distractors.why: Harrowby's motives stay hidden until a secondhand report from the housekeeper at the end.

distractors.text: keeping the narrator detached and free of any judgment of the others
distractors.why: The narrator states his judgment openly, calling Harrowby 'the coldest man in Skelwick'.

distractors.text: steady pride in a verdict he holds to this day
distractors.why: The ending shows he has since abandoned that verdict about Harrowby.

distractors.text: resentful anger at being deceived by Harrowby
distractors.why: The narrator shows no bitterness, and Harrowby never lied to him.

distractors.text: a plain note on his skill as a careful clerk
distractors.why: It does mention handwriting, but the retrospective context makes the remark ironic, not neutral.

distractors.text: stands for the Trust's rigid fairness in its dealings with fishermen
distractors.why: The scale belongs to Harrowby's private kitchen and household, not to the Trust.

distractors.text: hints that the housekeeper is shortchanging the boy who brings the fish
distractors.why: She pays four times the quay price, so no one is being cheated.

distractors.text: foretells the prosperity Venn will eventually gain from his fishing
distractors.why: The catch is tiny ('three small codling'); nothing suggests Venn will grow rich.
